title: The Servant at the Fairy's
subtitle: A dog corrects a servant's instructions

learningObjectives.text: What does the little dog tell the servant?
What should we avoid assuming from the title's word 'fairy'?

fairy.author: Basque storytellers; collected and translated by Wentworth Webster
fairy.translator: Wentworth Webster, with assistance from Julien Vinson and other local contributors
fairy.locator: THE SERVANT AT THE FAIRY'S.; THE SERVANT AT THE FAIRY'S., normalized characters 383-1279
fairy.excerpt: She gave her her morning's work to do, and said to her: "We are fairies. I must go from home, but your work is in the kitchen; smash the pitcher, break all the plates, pound the children, give them breakfast (by themselves), dirty their faces, and rumple their hair." [50] While she was at breakfast with the children, a little dog comes to her and says: "Tchau, tchau, tchow; I too, I want something." "Be off from here, silly little dog; I will give you a kick." But the dog did not go away; and at last she gave him something to eat--a little, not much. "And now," says he, "I will tell you what the mistress has told you to do. She told you to sweep the kitchen, to fill the pitcher, and to wash all the plates, and that if it is all well done she will give you the choice of a sack of charcoal or of a bag of gold; of a beautiful star on your forehead, or of a donkey's tail hanging from it.
fairy.note: Verbatim English text from Webster's second edition, collected chiefly in Labourd. The collection distinguishes local tales from French-derived contes des fées and compares some motifs with wider European stories.

narrativeBlocks.title: A new servant gets impossible instructions
narrativeBlocks.body: A young woman seeks work and is hired by a fairy. The mistress gives her a list of destructive tasks for the kitchen and children.

narrativeBlocks.title: The dog knows the real task
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (Webster's English collection; whitespace normalized): “She gave her her morning's work to do, and said to her: "We are fairies. But the dog did not go away; and at last she gave him something to eat--a little, not much. "And now," says he, "I will tell you what the mistress has told you to do. She told you to sweep the kitchen, to fill the pitcher, and to wash all the plates, and that if it is all well done she will give you the choice of a sack of charcoal or of a bag of gold; of a beautiful star on your forehead, or of a donkey's tail hanging from it.”

narrativeBlocks.title: Kindness changes the outcome
narrativeBlocks.body: After the servant feeds the little dog, it tells her the tasks she should actually do and what choices the fairy will offer.

narrativeBlocks.title: Do not overstate the supernatural label
narrativeBlocks.body: The title calls the being a fairy, within Webster's collected Basque tales. It is not evidence that all Basque communities used one uniform category called lamiñak.

narrativeBlocks.title: A familiar tale in a local collection
narrativeBlocks.body: This story appears in Webster's Basque collection, but the book also separates tales adapted directly from French. Its collection label alone does not prove an ancient or uniquely Basque origin.
